title: Use candles in an outage without starting a fire
summary: Candles light a room in an outage, and they start house fires when something that burns is too close, when one tips, or when people fall asleep with one lit. Use battery light first; when you do burn candles, put each in a sturdy holder on a metal tray, 30 cm (12 in) clear of anything that burns and with nothing above, in the room you're in, and snuff them before you sleep or leave.

materials.item: Candles: glass-jar (vigil or 7-day) candles or broad pillars first
materials.qty: as many as you need, but burn few at once

materials.item: Sturdy non-combustible holders, made for the candle size
Metal tray, baking sheet, frying pan or ceramic plate to stand them on
Snuffer, metal spoon or a lid that fits the jar
Lighter or matches, kept locked or up high
Scissors or nail clippers for trimming wicks
Battery smoke alarm in the room
Pan lid, baking sheet or fire blanket, and an ABC extinguisher if you have one

steps.text: Use flashlights, headlamps and battery lanterns first and keep candles for when the batteries run out. Ontario's Fire Marshal and the US Fire Administration both say use a flashlight, not a candle, for outage lighting (OFM candles, USFA candles).
steps.warn: Candles used for light, rather than decoration, appear to carry a greater risk of a fatal fire (NFPA FireDOC 2007).

steps.text: Pick the steadiest candles you have: candles in glass jars and broad pillars, which are hard to knock over (NCA outages). Skip thin tapers unless the holder grips them tightly and won't tip. Don't burn a candle whose wick has a metal core that leaves a grey mark when rubbed on white paper: it is probably lead (Health Canada candles).

Stand each candle in a sturdy holder that won't burn or tip, on a heat-resistant surface: a metal tray, baking sheet, frying pan or ceramic plate (NY OFPC candles, NCA outages). A candle you mean to keep lit for hours while you are awake goes in a glass jar standing on a metal tray or in a sink (NFPA religious candles).
steps.warn: Wooden and plastic holders can catch fire, and glass holders can crack when they get too hot (Health Canada candles).

steps.text: Place it at least 30 cm (12 in) from anything that burns: curtains, blinds, bedding, clothes, paper, books and furniture (OFM candles, NY OFPC candles). Nothing above it: no shelf, because the heat rises to it (Fire Scotland candles), and nothing hanging over it either, since NIST measured strong heat well above the flame (NIST candles). Keep it out of windows with curtains or blinds and out of draughts, vents and fan breezes, which blow things into the flame (NFPA religious candles, NY OFPC candles). Avoid candles in bedrooms and anywhere people may fall asleep (OFM candles, USFA candles).
steps.warn: Three in five US home candle fires start because something that burns was too close to the candle (Illinois SFM candles).

steps.text: Put candles up high, out of reach of children and pets, where nobody will bump them in the dark (NCA outages, Illinois SFM candles). Lock away or put up high the matches and lighters too (Illinois SFM candles).
steps.warn: Never leave a child alone in a room with a burning candle (Illinois SFM candles).

steps.text: Space candles at least 10 cm (4 in) apart (DSFRS candles). NY OFPC asks for at least 3 in (about 7.5 cm) so they don't melt each other or make their own draughts (NY OFPC candles).

Trim the wick to 5–7 mm (1/4 in) before lighting, and again every 2 to 3 hours to keep the flame low (Health Canada candles). Keep wick trimmings, matches and other bits out of the wax pool (NY OFPC candles, Health Canada candles).

Light it with your hair and sleeves held back (Illinois SFM candles). Don't light candles if you've been drinking or feel sleepy (Fire Scotland candles), and never where someone uses home oxygen (Illinois SFM candles).

Keep the people and the candles in one room so you can see every flame, and stay in that room. Don't carry a lit candle around or use one as a night light (NCA outages, NY OFPC candles). In a one-room household this is also the bedroom, so every candle is out before anyone lies down to sleep (OFM candles, USFA candles).
steps.warn: Falling asleep was a factor in 10% of US home candle fires and 12% of the deaths (Illinois SFM candles).

steps.text: Don't move a burning candle, or a jar or votive while its wax is liquid (Idaho SFM wax, NY OFPC candles). Put out a pillar when its wax pool reaches the outer edge (NY OFPC candles).
Stop burning a jar candle when about 1 cm (1/2 in) of wax is left, and a pillar when 5 cm (2 in) is left (NY OFPC candles).
steps.warn: Jar candles can shatter without warning as the wax gets low (DSFRS candles).

steps.text: Put every candle out before you sleep or leave the room (OFM candles, USFA candles). A snuffer, a metal spoon or a lid over the jar puts it out without spattering wax (RBFRS candles, NY OFPC candles, Idaho SFM wax). That includes 7-day and vigil candles: they are made to burn for days, but the advice is the same for every candle (OFM candles, USFA candles).
steps.warn: Never pour water on a candle: hot wax burns like grease and water spreads the flame (Idaho SFM wax, RBFRS candles).

steps.text: Keep working battery smoke alarms on every storey, outside each sleeping area and inside each bedroom, and test them every month (OFM candles for every storey and the monthly test; NFPA religious candles for outside sleeping areas and inside bedrooms). Ontario's handout asks for a CO alarm on every storey too (OFM candles). If you have a spare alarm, put one in the room where the candles burn.

notes:
## Why candles are the outage fire

- In the US, fire services get about 20 home candle fire calls a day. For 2015–2019, candles caused 2% of home fires and 3% of home fire deaths (Illinois SFM candles, citing NFPA).
- Three in five of those fires started because something that burns was left or came too close to the candle. 37% started in bedrooms and caused 35% of the deaths. December and January are the worst months (Illinois SFM candles).
- NFPA found that candles used for light, rather than decoration, appear to carry a greater risk of a fatal fire (NFPA FireDOC 2007). The candle makers' association, quoting NFPA, says more than 20% of fatal candle fires happen during a loss of power (NCA outages).
- Health Canada says there are no Canada-wide candle fire figures. From Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and BC data for 1999–2008, it estimates nearly 800 candle fires a year in Canada, with on average 8 deaths and 115 injuries a year (Health Canada candles).

The pattern is the same each time: the flame is near curtains, bedding or paper; a candle tips or is knocked over; or people fall asleep with candles lit. An outage adds dark rooms and tired people bundled in blankets close to the light.

## How much light and heat a candle really gives

| | One candle | For comparison |
|---|---|---|
| Light | About 1 candela; spread all round, roughly 12–13 lumens | A 60 W bulb gives about 800 lumens |
| Heat | About 77 W from a 21 mm paraffin taper (NIST candles) | See [Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm) |
| Wax burned | About 0.1 g a minute (about 6 g an hour) from that taper (NIST candles) | |

- **Light.** The candela, the unit of brightness, still matches roughly what a wax candle gives, and a full sphere is 4π steradians, so one candela all round is about 12.6 lumens (NIST candela). A 60 W incandescent bulb gives about 800 lumens (FEMP bulbs). By that arithmetic you'd need around 60 candles to match one ordinary bulb. One candle is enough to find your way round a room, not to read or work by for long.
- **Heat.** NIST burned a 21 mm (about 7/8 in) paraffin taper and measured about 77 W of heat, give or take 9 W, with a flame about 4 cm (1.6 in) tall. It burned down about 0.35 mm a minute, roughly 2 cm (3/4 in) an hour (NIST candles). A candle warms your hands, not a room. A clay flower-pot over candles adds no heat and has started house fires (AAP FactCheck); see [Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm) for the numbers.
- **Heat goes up.** Even 26 cm (10 in) above the candle base, NIST still measured about 10 kW/m² of heat flux (NIST candles). That is why Fire Scotland says never to put a candle under a shelf (Fire Scotland candles); anything hanging above one is in the same heat.
- **Air.** A candle flame that burns without visible soot burns its wax almost completely (NIST candles). A flickering, smoking flame doesn't: trim the wick and move it out of the draught (NY OFPC candles). Burn candles in a ventilated room (NY OFPC candles), and keep a CO alarm going anyway if any other fuel burns in the house; see [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).

## What to stock and how to burn it

| Candle | Good for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Glass jar (vigil, prayer or "7-day") | Long, steady burning; the flame sits inside the glass | Stand it on a metal tray or in a sink; stop with about 1 cm (1/2 in) of wax left, or the glass may crack or shatter (NFPA religious candles, NY OFPC candles, DSFRS candles) |
| Broad pillar | Hard to knock over (NCA outages) | Put it out when the wax pool reaches the edge (NY OFPC candles) |
| Tea light | Cheap, short burns | The foil cup gets hot enough to melt what it sits on (DSFRS candles) |
| Taper | Common in kitchen drawers and churches | Tall and thin, so easier to knock over than a broad pillar (NCA outages); needs a holder that grips it |

NFPA's advice for a candle that must burn continuously, for example for religious reasons, is the closest official advice for a candle you need lit for hours: in a glass container, standing in a sink, on a metal tray or in a deep basin of water (NFPA religious candles). It is not advice to leave one burning while you sleep.

Check salvaged and imported candles for lead wicks: a wick with a metal core that leaves a grey mark on white paper is probably lead, and burning it puts lead vapour and dust in the room, worst for children and pregnant women (Health Canada candles).

## Tea lights

Tea lights look harmless and cause a lot of fires.
- The thin metal cup gets very hot. Fire services warn it can melt plastic and the surface underneath, and start a fire (DSFRS candles, Fire Scotland candles).
- Never stand one straight on plastic or any surface that can melt or burn. Put it in a holder made for tea lights that won't burn and holds it upright, on a heat-resistant surface (Fire Scotland candles, DSFRS candles).
- Keep them at least 10 cm (4 in) apart (DSFRS candles).

## A tent or blanket den in the room

Pitching a tent or making a blanket den in the warm room is a good way to sleep warm (see [Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm)). Keep every candle out of it and away from it. CPSC says to treat tents and sleeping bags as flammable and never bring a candle, lantern or stove into a tent; candles have caused serious and fatal burns in tents, often when the camper fell asleep (CPSC camping). Devon and Somerset fire service says no candles in or near a tent (DSFRS candles).

## When a candle tips

1. **It went out as it fell:** leave it where it is and let the spilled wax harden before you clean it up. Don't grab a jar or votive full of liquid wax (NY OFPC candles, Idaho SFM wax).
2. **It's still burning on its side:** put it out with a snuffer, spoon, lid or baking sheet (RBFRS candles, Idaho SFM wax). No water (Idaho SFM wax).
3. **Something else has caught:** go to [When no help is coming](#ref/safety_candles/when_no_help_is_coming) below.
4. **Hot wax on skin:** cool it under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20, and leave wax that is stuck to the skin in place; see [Hot surfaces](#browse/hazards/burn).

Then ask why it tipped: a wobbly holder, a crowded table, a pet, a child or a draught. Fix that before you light it again.

## When no help is coming

Keep a pan lid or baking sheet, and a fire blanket or an ABC extinguisher if you have them, where candles burn.

- **A jar or wax pool on fire:** treat it like a grease fire. Slide a lid or baking sheet over it, or lay a fire blanket over it, and leave it. Tasmania Fire Service says to leave a blanket on a burning pan for at least 30 minutes (Tasmania FS blankets). Don't pick it up or move it while it burns or while the wax is liquid (Idaho SFM wax).
- **Never water on burning wax.** It spreads the flame onto anyone and anything nearby (Idaho SFM wax, RBFRS candles).
- **Burning paper, cloth or a tablecloth with no wax pool:** water or an ABC extinguisher works on ordinary burning materials; aim at the base and sweep (see [Which extinguisher](#ref/reference_fire_heat/which_extinguisher) and [Using one: PASS](#ref/reference_fire_heat/using_one_pass)).
- **Fight it only while it is small** and not spreading, with your way out behind you. Otherwise get everyone out, closing doors behind you (DSFRS candles), and stay out ([Fight or leave](#ref/reference_fire_heat/fight_or_leave)).
- **Clothes on fire:** stop, drop and roll, then cool the burns; see [Open flames](#browse/hazards/open_flame).
- **Afterwards:** anyone who breathed smoke goes into fresh air and is watched; see [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide). Before lighting candles again, light fewer of them, in one room, on trays, and get a smoke alarm working.
